Four stories. Four childhood dreams. One sky that brought us together.

Each of us found NASA through a different spark, but we share the same wonder: how far can curiosity take us?

“وَكُلٌّ فِي فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ” — each has an orbit, a place, a purpose.

We blend our passion for astronomy and space physics with AI, coding, data analysis, and design to turn big questions into real impact.

We are not here just to participate; we are here to build with purpose and compete to win—together.
summary:
BLOOM is an interactive Earth observation platform that connects information from space with meaningful questions on the ground, helping users explore and understand environmental change.
The pilot project focuses on two study areas (eastern and western polygons) in Jericho, Palestine, analyzing vegetation greenness (NDVI) and rainfall patterns over a 20-year period from 2005 to 2024. Powered by NASA MODIS and GPM IMERG data products and a Google Earth Engine workflow, the interactive web interface integrates mapping, historical observations, statistical analysis, area comparisons, exploratory models, and evidence reports.
Rather than simply showing where vegetation changes occur, BLOOM helps users investigate what those shifts mean while accounting for scientific uncertainty.
Looking ahead, BLOOM’s long-term vision is to make Earth observation data more accessible and develop transparent, explainable decision-support tools. Ultimately, the platform aims to compare smaller land areas to support agriculture, land planning, community-based environmental research, and informed local decision-making.

Page 1 — Cover

NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE 2026 / EARTH DETECTIVE

PROJECT DETAILS

A comprehensive technical and scientific account of the BLOOM environmental investigation prototype.

Jericho, Palestine | Study period 2005-2024 | Two mapped areas

Current stage: interactive research prototype; upstream data provenance review pending.

BLOOM / BEYOND THE GREEN

PROJECT SUBMISSION | 2026

Page 2 — Project Overview

PROJECT DETAILS / 01 / OVERVIEW

Project overview

From satellite observations to transparent, geographically grounded questions about environmental change.

The core problem

Earth observation missions provide extraordinary coverage of land conditions, yet a change in satellite-measured greenness does not automatically explain its cause. Rainfall variability, irrigation, crop cycles, harvesting, surface change, land-use decisions, and sensor or seasonal effects can produce related patterns. For many non-specialist users, the gap between receiving a number and understanding how to investigate it remains substantial.

The BLOOM response

BLOOM - Beyond the Green is an interactive Python/Streamlit prototype connecting a mapped research location, annual NDVI and rainfall datasets, statistical analysis, side-by-side area comparisons, and field-verification guidance. It is designed to communicate evidence and uncertainty together rather than declare a cause from one indicator.

What the project aims to achieve

  • Access: make Earth observation datasets understandable through a navigable web interface.
  • Context: keep spatial boundaries, dates, units, and source metadata beside environmental readings.
  • Investigation: compare multiple signals and use statistical methods as screening tools.
  • Responsibility: recommend what to verify on the ground before any intervention.
  • Scalability: establish a foundation for future finer-resolution, purpose-specific land comparisons.

Scope in this submission

The implemented study compares two documented polygon files in the Jericho area over the years 2005-2024. It is not currently a parcel-purchase recommender, construction-suitability checker, automatic environmental diagnosis, or validated field-impact study.

Page 3 — Study Design

PROJECT DETAILS / 02 / STUDY DESIGN

The Jericho pilot

An applied geographic investigation, not an abstract demonstration.

The pilot focuses on two study polygons in Jericho, Palestine. The eastern polygon is area_a (Area A), and the western polygon is area_b (Area B). Their coordinates are stored in the project GeoJSON file and used by the interface for selection, comparison, and visualization.

Figure 1. Study regions displayed over satellite imagery. The outline shapes are supplied study polygons; satellite basemap imagery is attributed to Esri and its imagery providers.

Study component

Specification

Location

Jericho, Palestine; Jordan Valley context

Study units

Two polygons: area_a (east) and area_b (west)

Observation window

2005-2024; 20 annual values per area in each primary CSV

Temporal comparison

Same year range and compatible area identifiers for vegetation and rainfall

Geospatial source

data/study_areas.geojson, two-feature GeoJSON FeatureCollection

Interpretation rule

The polygons are real geographic shapes in the uploaded files, but the original import-to-export geometry match and final land-use labels still require independent confirmation. No parcel boundary or agricultural land category is certified by this visualization.

Page 4 — Experience

PROJECT DETAILS / 03 / EXPERIENCE

The investigation journey

The application turns a technical workflow into a sequence non-specialists can follow.

01 / Explore

User interaction: Choose one of the two mapped study areas on the interactive map or through the area selector.

What is produced: A clear spatial focus and the corresponding annual observations.

02 / Time Machine

User interaction: Select a year from 2005-2024 and inspect historical differences.

What is produced: Year-specific polygon-mean NDVI shading, rainfall readings and before/after context.

03 / Analyze

User interaction: Open NDVI and rainfall charts and inspect statistical outputs.

What is produced: Time series, estimated slopes and trend-significance context.

04 / Compare

User interaction: Review both areas across a common time window.

What is produced: Shared-axis comparisons and quantified contrasts.

05 / Investigate

User interaction: Open Mystery Lab and examine model validation outcomes.

What is produced: Anomaly leads only if the rainfall model passes explicit safeguards.

06 / Plan

User interaction: Choose a criterion in Area Advisor and review ground-check guidance.

What is produced: A transparent study-area suggestion or no suggestion, plus a conditional field checklist.

07 / Report

User interaction: Download an investigation brief for the selected question.

What is produced: Evidence notes, limitations and follow-up tasks.

What a judge can demonstrate

In the live interface, move from a map click to a selected study year; inspect the associated NDVI and precipitation figures; open comparison and trend views; choose an Area Advisor objective; and download an investigation brief. Each step makes the study context more explicit, rather than introducing an unexplained “best area” score.

Design principle

Geography first, evidence second, interpretation third. The application intentionally allows an inconclusive result when data, model fit, or verification are insufficient.

Page 5 — Delivered Modules

PROJECT DETAILS / 04 / DELIVERED MODULES

What has been built

A modular multi-page product with scientific functions behind the visual interface.

Home

BLOOM identity, environmental research context, pilot discovery, and navigation to the investigation.

Explore

Interactive study-area selection, map visualization, annual observations and exploration tools.

Time Machine

Year navigation, stable NDVI color categories for polygon means, and comparisons with the baseline year.

Analytics

NDVI and rainfall history, summary measures, estimated trend metrics, charts and CSV exploration.

Compare

Two-area NDVI and rainfall plots on consistent timelines with trend comparison.

Mystery Lab

Exploratory annual rainfall-to-NDVI model, chronological holdout metrics and guarded anomaly flags.

Area Advisor

Criterion-specific area comparisons and explanations, including “no clear recommendation” when appropriate.

Action Pathway

Detect - Verify - Act if confirmed - Measure sequence, field-check tasks and conditional follow-up.

Reports

Downloadable Markdown investigation notes with source status, result context, caveats and area guidance.

About

Scientific methodology, source descriptions, uncertainty statements and team workflow.

Key safeguards inside the interface

  • Synthetic demonstration values are separated from uploaded study files; demo values are not relabeled as NASA measurements.
  • The map shading describes each polygon's annual mean NDVI, not a full-resolution NDVI raster.
  • The advisor compares only the two available study areas and only against a user-selected research question.
  • User-entered checklist answers and proposed field clues are not represented as independently verified observations.

Page 6 — NASA Data and Supporting Tools

PROJECT DETAILS / 05 / DATA PRODUCTS

NASA data and supporting tools

The repository identifies specific satellite products and distinguishes data sources from processing and research references.

NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 v6.1

Role in BLOOM: Declared vegetation source; NDVI time series.

Important details: 16-day vegetation-index composites; approximate 250 m nominal native resolution; QA mask and scaling specified in export code.

NASA GPM IMERG Monthly V07

Role in BLOOM: Declared rainfall source; annual precipitation context.

Important details: Monthly precipitation rate in mm/hour converted to annual depth; nominal pixel size about 11.1 km.

NASA POWER API

Role in BLOOM: Separate supporting point reference near Jericho.

Important details: IMERG_PRECTOT daily precipitation aggregated by year; not a substitute for polygon-based GPM means.

Google Earth Engine

Role in BLOOM: Geospatial processing and export workflow.

Important details: JavaScript script identifies two study polygons, reduces MODIS and GPM collections, and exports CSV/GeoJSON.

NASA Giovanni

Role in BLOOM: Supporting research and visualization resource.

Important details: Not evidenced as the application's live extraction API or direct source of every plotted value.

NASA Earthdata / Earth Observatory / USGS Landsat

Role in BLOOM: Catalog, imagery and scientific background references.

Important details: Cited for context and methods; not claimed as proven direct inputs to the primary study-area CSVs.

Where the data live

The live interface reads annual CSV and geometry files committed to the repository rather than requesting a new satellite image from NASA on every interaction. Source identifiers, processing assumptions, validation checks, and provenance state are documented in data/metadata.json and the repository documents.

Why this distinction matters

NASA data-product catalogs describe what each product contains; they do not, by themselves, authenticate the origin of the specific CSV files uploaded to this repository. This report identifies both the intended NASA data products and the current provenance limitations.

Page 7 — Data Pipeline

PROJECT DETAILS / 06 / DATA PIPELINE

From observation to annual files

The documented extraction script defines repeatable calculations for each area and year.

1. Define the spatial units

The Earth Engine JavaScript script expects a two-polygon geometry imported as areaA. It assigns the eastern polygon to area_a and the western polygon to area_b, then creates a FeatureCollection using stable area identifiers.

2. Prepare vegetation measurements

The code filters the MODIS/061/MOD13Q1 image collection to 2005-2024 and the study footprints. For each image, it selects high-quality pixels using SummaryQA == 0, multiplies the original NDVI band by 0.0001, calculates a study-area mean, and then averages valid image means within each calendar year. The resulting value is unitless.

3. Prepare precipitation estimates

The code selects NASA/GPM_L3/IMERG_MONTHLY_V07 precipitation estimates. It converts each monthly mean rate from mm/hour into a monthly depth by multiplying by the actual number of hours in that month, spatially averages over the study polygon, and sums the twelve monthly depths to obtain annual mm. Incomplete annual records remain missing, not zero.

4. Export tabular and geographic files

File

Expected contents

data/ndvi_annual.csv

year, area_id, ndvi, valid_observations; 40 uploaded rows

data/rainfall_annual.csv

year, area_id, rainfall_mm, valid_months; 40 uploaded rows

data/study_areas.geojson

GeoJSON FeatureCollection with two named polygon features

data/metadata.json

Source descriptions, resolution, aggregation, verification and limitations

Aggregation caveat

The annual NDVI calculation averages valid composite-level spatial means; it is not equivalent to a fully spatially and temporally weighted pixel mean. Likewise, a coarse GPM value should not be interpreted as parcel-scale rainfall.

Page 8 — Methods

PROJECT DETAILS / 07 / METHODS

Trend testing and Mystery Lab

Statistical analysis is used to ask better questions, not to imply certainty.

Long-term trend analysis

The trend module works on one area and one variable at a time. Linear regression estimates an annual slope and a per-decade change rate. A Mann-Kendall test examines evidence of a monotonic trend. The prototype uses a significance convention of p < 0.05 when the test can be evaluated; a non-significant result does not prove that an area is stable.

Anomaly analysis: rainfall-based model

Mystery Lab fits a linear relationship between annual rainfall and NDVI for a selected study area. Its training and validation years are intentionally separated in time.

Validation element

Implemented rule

Chronological split

Training: 2005-2018; evaluation: 2019-2024, when complete data are available.

Minimum pairing

At least 10 valid training pairs and 3 validation pairs required.

Model performance

Holdout R-squared must be positive and mean absolute error must beat the training-mean baseline.

Candidate anomaly

A validation residual exceeding twice the training-residual sample standard deviation.

Failure behavior

Return insufficient evidence and no defensible anomaly alert if safeguards fail.

What an anomaly can and cannot mean

A difference between expected and observed NDVI is a signal for closer examination. It does not identify irrigation, crop damage, land-cover conversion, or any single cause. Annual rainfall is only one potential explanatory variable, and the two satellite products operate at different spatial resolutions.

Scientific standard

Exploratory models must not be evaluated on the same observations used to fit them. BLOOM therefore uses a chronological holdout and reports model quality before considering residual-based flags.

Page 9 — Observations

PROJECT DETAILS / 08 / OBSERVATIONS

What the uploaded files show

Examples below describe repository values and are deliberately separated from independent NASA-source verification.

The descriptive endpoint pattern is noteworthy: in the uploaded NDVI table, Area B has the higher annual mean in 2005, while Area A has the higher annual mean in 2024. BLOOM can surface this reversal as a discovery question, while leaving the cause open.

How to read the maps and figures

  • A colored polygon represents the mean annual NDVI value associated with that entire study polygon. It does not depict detailed within-field or within-parcel variability.
  • Year-to-year differences may reflect several competing mechanisms; endpoint comparison alone is not a significance test.
  • Rainfall figures are estimates and may be spatially similar across adjacent polygons because the GPM resolution is coarse.
  • These numbers are reproduced from uploaded CSVs; they have not been independently authenticated against original Earth Engine export artifacts.

Evidence status: provisional

The source validation report confirms acceptable structure, full recorded year coverage and values within expected bounds. It explicitly does not establish the original NASA extraction provenance. No observed difference here should be described as a confirmed environmental cause, yield outcome, or demonstrated benefit.

Page 10 — Decision Support

PROJECT DETAILS / 09 / DECISION SUPPORT

Area Advisor and Action Pathway

The prototype offers question-specific investigation guidance rather than a universal ranking of land.

Area Advisor criteria

Which is greener in a selected year?

How the comparison works: Compare the two uploaded polygon-mean NDVI values for that year.

Interpretation boundary: Higher NDVI is not equivalent to better farming suitability or higher crop yield.

Which has stronger supported greening?

How the comparison works: Compare per-decade linear slopes, with an area-specific increasing-trend significance check.

Interpretation boundary: The current check does not test whether the two slopes differ significantly from each other.

Where should we check first?

How the comparison works: Prioritize the polygon with lower recent mean NDVI over the selected short window.

Interpretation boundary: A follow-up priority is a screening clue, not a diagnosis of damage.

Evidence-to-action workflow

Detect: inspect selected NDVI and rainfall readings and the observed change. Verify: request field photographs, crop history, land use, water access and other relevant local checks. Act if confirmed: provide conditional suggestions that depend on a ground-supported explanation, potentially involving local specialists. Measure: compare new observations against a meaningful baseline without claiming the intervention succeeded before measurements exist.

Generated outputs

Area Advisor produces an explanation and report of the selected criterion. The Action Pathway generates an investigation plan and user-editable checklist. Reports can combine study context, trend outputs, model state, cautious interpretation, and proposed next steps in downloadable Markdown form.

Important boundary

This system does not currently approve land purchases, certify agricultural productivity, determine construction feasibility, or substitute for legal planning and technical due diligence.

Page 11 — Implementation

PROJECT DETAILS / 10 / IMPLEMENTATION

Software architecture

A Python-based, modular prototype with independently testable scientific and interface components.

The principal interface is ui_app.py, a Streamlit multipage application. A standalone investigation_app.py is also present for pilot investigation workflows; app.py remains a foundation entry point. Most scientific functionality is placed in reusable modules rather than embedded directly in the page layouts.

Repository path

Responsibility

ui_app.py

Primary navigation, sidebar controls, study selection and data-context setup.

investigation_app.py

Standalone pilot interface for geographic inquiry and area recommendations.

modules/ui_pages/

Home, Explore, Analytics, Mystery Lab, Compare, Reports, About and pilot UI elements.

modules/investigation_case.py

Load provisional uploaded study files, map clicks to polygons and prepare research briefs.

modules/ui_data.py / ui_pilot_context.py

Separate demo mode and provisional uploaded datasets from the strict verification contract.

modules/discovery_time_machine.py

Historical comparison, annual snapshot state and stable NDVI color bins.

modules/trend_analysis.py

Linear trends, Mann-Kendall testing and diagnostic return values.

modules/mystery_engine.py

Chronological holdout and gated exploratory residual analysis.

modules/area_advisor.py / action_planner.py

Criterion-specific screening, field checks and conditional actions.

scripts/ / data/ / docs/ / tests/

Extraction, study files, scientific provenance, quality tests and documentation.

Technology choices

Interface: Streamlit and custom CSS. Maps: Folium, Streamlit-Folium, GeoJSON, Esri satellite basemap imagery. Charts: Plotly. Computation: Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and pymannkendall. Data preparation: Google Earth Engine JavaScript. Repository and testing: GitHub, pytest and Python compilation checks.

Page 12 — Scientific QA

PROJECT DETAILS / 11 / SCIENTIFIC QA

Quality, provenance and limitations

BLOOM documents both what was checked and which evidence is still missing.

Checks completed on committed files

  • NDVI and rainfall CSVs contain 40 records each: 20 years for each of two study-area IDs, with unique area-year pairs.
  • NDVI values fall within the allowed [-1, 1] range; valid_observations are positive integers within the documented limit.
  • Annual precipitation values are nonnegative, and all uploaded annual rows list 12 valid months.
  • The GeoJSON contains a two-feature polygon collection, with closed outer rings and coordinate ranges in the Jericho vicinity.

Open questions before source authentication

Verification requirement

Current repository status

Original Earth Engine tasks, dates, account and task IDs

Not recorded in the metadata file.

Original export outputs compared with committed CSVs

No independently documented full-file or checksum comparison.

Polygon imports and exact extraction-footprint match

Not independently established.

Independent rerun of extraction and method review

Pending.

Confirmed land-use classification of both study areas

Not independently substantiated.

Scientific and operational limitations

MODIS and GPM have strongly different source resolutions (approximately 250 m versus 11.1 km); small nearby polygons may share rainfall pixels. Annual averages hide seasonality and intra-area variation. Possible mixed pixels, missing explanatory variables, model assumptions, multiple comparisons and serial correlation may affect statistical conclusions.

Publication boundary

The metadata currently states verification_status = pending. The application is designed to display provisional uploaded observations with explicit qualification and to prevent synthetic fixtures from being presented as NASA data. Source verification should be completed before publication of authenticated observational claims.

Page 13 — Reproducibility

PROJECT DETAILS / 12 / REPRODUCIBILITY

How to run and review BLOOM

The repository includes code, test coverage, dataset descriptions and a documented extraction workflow.

Install and launch

The main application can be started with the commands below in a Python environment with the required dependencies installed:

git clone https://github.com/heba-mustafa59/bloom-nasa.git
cd bloom-nasa
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m streamlit run ui_app.py

Other useful entry points

  • Standalone pilot: python -m streamlit run investigation_app.py
  • Automated tests: python -m pytest -q
  • NASA POWER point retrieval: python scripts/fetch_nasa_power.py
  • Earth Engine export: inspect scripts/export_nasa_data.js in Google Earth Engine Code Editor. The required source polygon geometry must be supplied and checked.

Review checklist

Confirm that the area selector matches the displayed GeoJSON polygons; verify the annual values against the CSVs; inspect the full time window and year-step controls; run unit/integration tests; review report provenance statements; and test source links and map attribution in the deployed environment.

Page 14 — Impact

PROJECT DETAILS / 13 / IMPACT

Who could benefit and how

The project is designed to make existing scientific information easier to investigate and communicate.

Students and educators

Current value of the prototype: A navigable example of interpreting historical Earth observations with their limitations.

Future opportunity: Teaching resources and additional geographic case studies.

Environmental researchers

Current value of the prototype: Area comparison, time-series inspection, trend assessment and documentation.

Future opportunity: More variables, seasonal resolution, validation and export choices.

Farmers and local communities

Current value of the prototype: Accessible mapped evidence and structured questions for field follow-up.

Future opportunity: Locally informed decisions supported by on-the-ground observations.

Land buyers and planners

Current value of the prototype: A demonstration of how observations can support a broader investigation.

Future opportunity: Parcel-scale comparisons with suitable data, regulated planning context and professional validation.

What makes BLOOM different

  • Connected layers: study area, year, NDVI, rainfall, trends, model checks and reports are handled within one research journey.
  • Evidence before alerts: the anomaly model can refuse to produce flags when predictive validation is weak.
  • Transparent advice: the advisor makes only goal-specific, interpretable comparisons and explains caveats.
  • Field orientation: the action workflow asks what should be verified and what outcomes would need future measurement.

Impact is a goal, not an invented result

This prototype has not been evaluated for real-world adoption, user decision quality, yield improvement, restoration outcomes, or financial savings. The impact described above is the problem it aims to address and the capabilities it makes available for further testing.

Page 15 — Roadmap

PROJECT DETAILS / 14 / ROADMAP

From regional research to parcel insight

The longer-term concept extends BLOOM toward smaller areas and goal-specific land comparisons.

Now - working prototype

Development priority: Two Jericho study polygons; map, history, statistical investigation, advisor and reporting.

Evidence requirements: Documented uploaded files; current provenance review still open.

Next - geographic expansion

Development priority: Additional cities, more documented study regions, richer timeline controls and new independent variables.

Evidence requirements: Reproducible geospatial extraction, consistent IDs, source records and QA.

Later - smaller parcels

Development priority: Parcel-scale imagery, boundary selection, soil and water context, infrastructure and hazards.

Evidence requirements: Suitable resolution, cadastral/legal boundaries, local data and expert review.

Later - explainable guidance

Development priority: User chooses an objective, such as agriculture versus construction, and compares evidence for multiple candidate sites.

Evidence requirements: Criterion-specific decision models, validation, uncertainty disclosure and regulatory checks.

Ongoing - ground feedback

Development priority: Field photos, local observations, community confirmations and intervention monitoring.

Evidence requirements: Consent, provenance, geolocation accuracy, reviewer workflows and measured follow-up.

Future example: comparing land before purchase

A person interested in buying land could eventually compare two selected parcels. For agricultural purposes, the platform would need more than annual NDVI: crop history, soil properties, water access and locally relevant agronomic constraints. For construction, the relevant factors would differ: zoning, parcel title, terrain, flood risk, access, utilities and professional engineering assessment.

The future recommendation should be an explainable comparison against the user's intended purpose, not an automatic declaration that one plot is universally “better.”

Technical feasibility boundary

Current 250 m MODIS vegetation data and roughly 11 km GPM rainfall estimates cannot resolve many individual land parcels or authorize construction decisions. Smaller-scale functionality requires other data sources and independent local verification.
